questions.q: Billroth I gastrectomy is a:
opts: Distal gastrectomy with an end to end gastroduodenal anastomosis
Subtotal gastrectomy with an end to side gastrojejunal anastomosis
Total gastrectomy with a Roux loop
questions.exp: Billroth I gastrectomy: distal gastrectomy with end to end gastro-duodenal anastomosis. (Book p157)

questions.q: Billroth II (Polya) reconstruction is performed after:
questions.exp: Billroth II gastrectomy / Polya reconstruction: subtotal/partial gastrectomy. (Book p157)

questions.q: In a Billroth II (Polya) reconstruction the duodenum is:
opts: Anastomosed end to end to the stomach
questions.exp: Billroth II: close the duodenal stump and perform an end to side gastro-jejunal anastomosis. (Book p157)

questions.q: The anastomosis created in a Billroth II (Polya) reconstruction is:
questions.exp: Billroth II: end to side gastro-jejunal anastomosis. (Book p157)

questions.q: In a Billroth II reconstruction, bile and pancreatic juice pass through the:
questions.exp: Billroth II: afferent loop carries bile and pancreatic juice; efferent loop carries food. (Book p157)

questions.q: The limb that carries food in a Billroth II reconstruction is the:
questions.exp: Food passes through the efferent loop. (Book p157)

questions.q: In a Roux-en-Y gastrojejunostomy the duodenal stump is:
questions.exp: Roux en Y gastrojejunostomy / gastric bypass: closed duodenal stump, Roux limb and BP limb. (Book p157)

questions.q: The length of the Roux limb used in a Roux-en-Y reconstruction is:
questions.exp: Roux limb: 50 cm of jejunum. (Book p158)

questions.q: The limb carrying bile and pancreatic secretions in a Roux-en-Y reconstruction is the:
questions.exp: Roux-en-Y: Roux limb (50 cm) with a bilio-pancreatic (BP) limb. (Book p158)

questions.q: A retrocolic Roux limb is placed:
opts: Behind the colon, through the transverse mesocolon
questions.exp: Retrocolic: behind the colon, through the transverse mesocolon. (Book p158)

questions.q: An antecolic Roux limb is placed:
questions.exp: Antecolic: in front of the colon. (Book p158)

questions.q: Petersen's hernia after a Roux-en-Y reconstruction is bowel herniating:
questions.exp: Petersen hernia: bowel herniation behind the Roux limb. (Book p158)

questions.q: Stemmer's hernia after gastric reconstruction is bowel herniating:
questions.exp: Stemmer's hernia: bowel herniation through the transverse mesocolon window. (Book p158)

questions.q: Internal hernias after gastric reconstruction include:
questions.exp: Internal hernias: Stemmer's hernia (through transverse mesocolon) and Petersen's hernia (behind Roux limb). (Book p160)

questions.q: Vagotomy is:
opts: Not routinely done, having been replaced by proton pump inhibitors
The first line treatment for all peptic ulcers
questions.exp: Cutting the vagus is not routinely done - it has been replaced by PPIs. (Book p158)

questions.q: Indications for vagotomy include:
opts: Duodenal ulcers and type 2 and 3 gastric ulcers
questions.exp: Indications: duodenal ulcers; type 2 and 3 gastric ulcers. (Book p158)

questions.q: The anterior nerve of Latarjet terminates as the:
questions.exp: Anterior nerve of Latarjet continues as the crow's foot, which supplies the antrum. (Book p158)

questions.q: Cutting the motor branch to the gallbladder during vagotomy leads to:
questions.exp: Posterior trunk gives a motor branch to the gallbladder; if cut it can lead to GB stasis and stone formation. (Book p158)

questions.q: Cutting the motor branch to the pylorus results in:
opts: Impaired gastric emptying requiring a drainage procedure
questions.exp: Motor branch to pylorus: if cut, impaired gastric emptying - a drainage procedure is required. (Book p158)

questions.q: The nerve responsible for ulcer recurrence after vagotomy is the:
questions.exp: Criminal nerve of Grassi: responsible for ulcer recurrence after vagotomy. (Book p158)

questions.q: Drainage procedures performed along with vagotomy are:
questions.exp: Drainage procedures: gastrojejunostomy and pyloroplasty (pyloroplasty renders the pylorus incompetent). (Book p158)

questions.q: In truncal vagotomy, the distal esophagus is skeletonised for:
questions.exp: Truncal vagotomy: distal 6-8 cm of the esophagus is skeletonised. (Book p159)

questions.q: Highly selective vagotomy denervates:
opts: Branches to the body and fundus while sparing the antrum and pylorus
The whole stomach including the pylorus
questions.exp: HSV: branches to the body and fundus are cut; denervation is stopped 7 cm proximal to the pylorus, sparing the pylorus and antrum. (Book p159)

questions.q: In highly selective vagotomy, denervation is stopped how far proximal to the pylorus?
questions.exp: Denervation is stopped 7 cm proximal to the pylorus. (Book p159)

questions.q: The nerve spared in a highly selective vagotomy is the:
questions.exp: HSV: anterior nerve of Latarjet is spared. (Book p159)

questions.q: Compared with other vagotomies, highly selective vagotomy has:
opts: The fewest complications but a higher ulcer recurrence rate
The most complications and the lowest recurrence
questions.exp: HSV: fewer complications, but ulcer recurrence is higher; acid reduction is less. (Book p159)

questions.q: The lowest ulcer recurrence rate is achieved with:
questions.exp: Truncal vagotomy with antrectomy gives the greatest acid reduction and the least recurrence. (Book p159)

questions.q: Truncal vagotomy with antrectomy is indicated for:
opts: Gastric outlet obstruction due to cancer
questions.exp: Indications: truncal vagotomy with antrectomy is used for recurrent ulcers. (Book p159)

questions.q: The m/c nutritional complication after gastric reconstruction is:
questions.exp: Nutritional complications: iron deficiency anaemia is the m/c (microcytic hypochromic anaemia). (Book p159)

questions.q: The peripheral smear in post-gastrectomy iron deficiency anaemia shows:
questions.exp: Iron deficiency anaemia: peripheral smear shows microcytic hypochromic anaemia. (Book p159)

questions.q: Vitamin B12 deficiency after gastric surgery presents with:
opts: Easy fatigability, neuropathy and megaloblastic anaemia
questions.exp: Vitamin B12 deficiency: easy fatigability, neuropathy, megaloblastic anaemia. (Book p159)

questions.q: Nutritional complications after gastric reconstruction include all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.exp: Nutritional complications: iron deficiency anaemia, vitamin B12 deficiency, calcium deficiency. (Book p159)

questions.q: Duodenal stump blowout is seen in:
questions.exp: Duodenal stump blowout: seen in Polya and Roux en Y reconstruction. (Book p159)

questions.q: Duodenal stump blowout typically presents on post-operative day:
questions.exp: Duodenal stump blowout presents on post-operative day 4. (Book p159)

questions.q: The features of duodenal stump blowout are:
questions.exp: Duodenal stump blowout: abdominal pain, fever, peritonitis. (Book p159)

questions.q: Haemorrhage after gastric reconstruction occurs from:
questions.exp: Hemorrhage: from the anastomotic site. (Book p159)

questions.q: Marginal (anastomotic) peptic ulcers after gastric surgery occur because:
opts: Acid from the stomach passes directly into the jejunum
questions.exp: Peptic ulcers: acid from the stomach goes directly into the jejunum causing ulcers. (Book p159)

questions.q: Afferent loop syndrome is a complication of:
questions.exp: Afferent loop syndrome: seen in Polya reconstruction. (Book p159)

questions.q: Afferent loop syndrome is caused by:
opts: Twisting of the afferent loop causing obstruction and perforation
Internal herniation behind the Roux limb
questions.exp: Afferent loop syndrome: twisting of the afferent loop leads to obstruction and perforation. (Book p159)

questions.q: Dumping syndrome is m/c after:
opts: Polya (Billroth II) reconstruction, more than Roux-en-Y
questions.exp: Dumping syndrome: m/c with Polya > Roux-en-Y. (Book p160)

questions.q: Early dumping is caused by:
opts: Rapid influx of fluid into the bowel due to hyperosmolar contents
Excess insulin release after delayed sugar absorption
questions.exp: Early dumping: rapid influx of fluid due to hyperosmolar contents in the bowel. (Book p160)

questions.q: Features of early dumping include all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.exp: Early dumping: nausea, vomiting, bloating, headache, sweating, tachycardia; starts 10-15 mins after food and worsens with food. (Book p160)

questions.q: Late dumping is due to:
opts: Excess insulin release causing rebound hypoglycaemia
Rapid fluid shifts into the bowel
questions.exp: Late dumping: reduced absorption of sugar but complete insulin release - excess insulin causes rebound hypoglycemia. (Book p160)

questions.q: Late dumping occurs how long after a meal?
questions.exp: Late dumping: onset 30-40 mins after food, relieved by rest and improves with food. (Book p160)

questions.q: Early dumping begins how long after a meal?
questions.exp: Early dumping: onset 10-15 mins after food. (Book p160)

questions.q: Dietary management of dumping syndrome includes all of the following EXCEPT:
opts: Large meals with plenty of liquid
A high fat and high protein diet
questions.exp: Dietary recommendations: avoid large meals, avoid liquids with meals, avoid sugar rich liquids, small frequent meals, high fat and protein diet. (Book p160)

questions.q: Persistent dumping despite an anti-dumping diet is treated with:
questions.exp: Persistent dumping in spite of an anti-dumping diet: octreotide. (Book p160)

questions.q: If dumping syndrome persists despite dietary measures and octreotide, the next step is:
questions.exp: If medical measures fail: convert to Roux-en-Y. (Book p160)

units.title: Gastrectomy Reconstructions: Billroth I & II
units.sec: Gastrectomy Reconstructions: Billroth I & II · p157
units.guide: Billroth I is the physiological option - distal gastrectomy with an end-to-end gastroduodenal join. Billroth II (Polya) closes the duodenal stump and joins the stomach end-to-side to jejunum, creating an afferent limb that carries bile and pancreatic juice and an efferent limb that carries food.

units.title: Roux-en-Y Reconstruction
units.guide: Roux-en-Y also closes the duodenal stump but separates the streams: a 50 cm Roux limb carries food, a bilio-pancreatic limb carries bile and pancreatic juice. The Roux limb can be routed retrocolic (behind the colon, through the transverse mesocolon) or antecolic (in front of the colon).

units.title: Internal Hernias after Reconstruction
units.guide: Two internal hernias to name after reconstruction: Petersen's, where bowel slips behind the Roux limb, and Stemmer's, where it slips through the window in the transverse mesocolon.

units.title: Vagotomy: Branches & Indications
units.guide: Vagotomy is rarely needed now that PPIs exist, but when it is done it is for duodenal ulcers or type 2 and 3 gastric ulcers. Know the wiring: the anterior trunk continues as the anterior nerve of Latarjet and its crow's foot to the antrum with a motor branch to the pylorus (cut it and the stomach will not empty, so add a drainage procedure); the posterior trunk gives a coeliac branch, a gallbladder branch (cut it and stones form) and the posterior nerve of Latarjet; the criminal nerve of Grassi is the one left behind that brings the ulcer back.

units.title: Types of Vagotomy
units.guide: Truncal vagotomy skeletonises the distal 6-8 cm of esophagus and needs drainage (gastrojejunostomy or pyloroplasty). Highly selective vagotomy cuts only the branches to the body and fundus, stops 7 cm short of the pylorus and spares the nerve of Latarjet - so no drainage, fewer complications, but more recurrences; truncal vagotomy with antrectomy reduces acid most and recurs least.

units.title: Nutritional Complications after Gastric Surgery
units.sec: Nutritional Complications after Gastric Surgery · p159
units.guide: Expect iron deficiency (microcytic hypochromic, and the commonest), then B12 deficiency with neuropathy and megaloblastic anaemia, then calcium deficiency.

units.title: Surgical Complications of Reconstruction
units.guide: Duodenal stump blowout belongs to Polya and Roux-en-Y and strikes around day 4 with pain, fever and peritonitis; bleeding comes from the anastomosis; acid hitting jejunum directly causes marginal ulcers; and in a Polya the afferent loop can twist, obstruct and perforate.

units.title: Dumping Syndrome
units.guide: Dumping is commonest after Polya. Early dumping (10-15 minutes) is the osmotic fluid shift - nausea, bloating, sweating, tachycardia, worse with food. Late dumping (30-40 minutes) is excess insulin after rapid sugar absorption - rebound hypoglycaemia that food actually relieves. Treat with small frequent low-sugar, high-fat and high-protein meals, then octreotide, then conversion to Roux-en-Y.
